titulo.texto: Stela of Quetzalcóatl from Castillo de Teayo

frase_gancho.texto: Ehécatl, the god of the wind, carved where the Huastec and Mexica worlds met.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the wind that moves the clouds, we move on to the final destiny of us all. Before leaving the hall, step out into the garden and look for a figure seated on a throne, so thin that it looks almost like a skeleton, with human skulls on its headdress.

guion_corto.texto: Ehécatl means “wind,” and this stela shows the god of the wind standing, with a tall cone-shaped headdress called a copilli. Over his mouth he wears a mask, on his chest an ornament of cut sea shell, the ehecacózcatl, and at his waist a cloth skirt. It comes from Castillo de Teayo, in northern Veracruz, and dates to the Late Postclassic, the last centuries before the arrival of the Spaniards. It is a Huastec work with a strong Mexica imprint. That is why it helps us understand how far the Mexica empire reached on the Gulf Coast: it is thought that, in that area, the Mexica established a strategic colony.

guion_largo.texto:
How do you sculpt the wind? You can’t. What you can do is sculpt its signs, and this stela does so with three: a mask over the mouth, a cut shell on the chest, and a cone-shaped headdress. That is enough to know that you are standing before Ehécatl, the god of the wind.

His name is Nahuatl and means, simply, “wind.” Here it appears joined to another name: Ehécatl-Quetzalcóatl, the form of Quetzalcóatl as the god of the wind. He is the same god as the [Feathered Serpent](mna_s04_templo_quetzalcoatl) you saw in Teotihuacán and in Tula, but with a human body. According to a Nahua myth, it was he who blew to set the Sun in motion, and the world began to move.

Go over his attributes one by one. The mask covering his mouth recalls a bird’s beak, and it is the way he is almost always drawn: the god who blows. On his chest he wears the ehecacózcatl, the “jewel of the wind,” a sea shell cut in a spiral, the same symbol you saw on the merlons of Tula and on the bronze shell in the courtyard. And on his head, the copilli, a tall, conical headdress, which in Nahuatl is also the word for “crown.” A cloth skirt completes the attire.

This stela comes from Castillo de Teayo, a site in northern Veracruz. Its modern name was given by the Spaniards after “El Castillo,” a pyramid of several tiers. Around it, sculptures of gods that you already know or will come to know have been found, such as Tláloc, [Xipe Tótec](mna_s04_xipe_totec) and maize deities, which says a great deal about what people asked of the gods in that region: rain, renewal, and good harvests.

Teayo lies in Huastec land. The Huastecs inhabited the northern Gulf Coast and spoke a Mayan language, Teenek, which their descendants still speak today. You will see this when you go up to the ethnography halls. Even so, in the Late Postclassic, the Mexica empire extended its power as far as this part of the coast. For that reason, specialists see in the stela a blend: an upright, freestanding figure in the local style, with an iconography of gods that comes from central Mexico.

What were the Mexica doing here? It is thought that, in that area, they established a strategic colony, a place from which to watch over the routes and secure the products of the coast: cotton, cacao, feathers, and other goods that reached Tenochtitlan as tribute. We do not know all the details, and specialists continue to debate how much was conquest and how much was exchange.

That is why this piece tells more than a story of gods. It can be read as a sign of how the power of Tenochtitlan reached far beyond its island and blended with local styles. The gods traveled with the armies, with the merchants, and with the tribute, and each region dressed them in its own way.

Before moving on, look again at the headdress, the mask, and the shell. In ancient Mexico, the wind was not a detail of the weather: it opened the way for the rains, set the Sun in motion, and gave breath to the shells that called people to the rituals. Whoever carved this stone wanted you to feel a gust as you passed in front of it.

texto.pregunta: Myth: Quetzalcóatl is always depicted as a feathered serpent.
texto.respuesta: Reality: He was also depicted as Ehécatl, the wind god, in human form, with a tall headdress and a mask over his mouth, as in this stela.
